item.title: SherlockEQ 0.2.0
item.description:
SherlockEQ 0.2.0

The first feature release since 0.1: Listening Comfort — level-dependent processing that shapes sound only while it needs it, instead of permanently re-tuning the curve. Soften a harsh "sss," ease shouty midrange, or lift dialogue over a score — each engages when the triggering sound is present and relaxes when it's gone. Per ear, zero added latency, and the peak limiter stays the ceiling over any boost.

Added

  • Listening Comfort panel. A new sidebar section with three named, preconfigured processors — Speech Presence, Harshness Control, and Sibilance Tamer. Each is just an on/off, a Strength slider, and a Sensitivity slider, with a live activity meter showing how much it's working in the moment. Independent per ear, with the same Separate L/R switch the rest of the app uses.
  • Adaptive, level-independent triggering. Each processor measures its target band against a slow rolling average of that band, so it behaves the same on a quiet podcast and a loud movie — no SPL calibration required. Sensitivity sets how far above that average it reacts; Strength sets how much it does.
  • Dynamics overlay on the Expert canvas. A new Dynamics layer chip draws each active processor's response live, moving under your static EQ curve, so you can watch the comfort tools engage against the spectrum in real time.

Changed

  • Reference Mode and the chain bypass now cover the comfort tools. Reference Mode (⌘B / the title-bar toggle) drops the Listening Comfort stage along with the rest of the chain, so your A/B is still a true comparison against the unprocessed source. A dedicated per-stage toggle lets you turn the comfort tools off while keeping your EQ, headphone correction, and notch active.

Fixed

  • Menu-bar popover lingered behind the main window. Opening the full app from the popover now closes the popover instead of leaving it floating in front of the window.

Not a medical device

SherlockEQ is not a healthcare or medical application. It does not diagnose, treat, measure, or monitor any hearing condition, tinnitus, or disability. The Listening Comfort tools shape audio for comfort and clarity — they are not a hearing aid. For concerns about your hearing, consult a doctor, audiologist, or licensed healthcare professional.

item.title: SherlockEQ 0.1.4
item.description:
SherlockEQ 0.1.4

A look-and-feel release. A new app icon, a Liquid Glass pass over the whole window on macOS Tahoe, and Reference Mode promoted to the title bar so you can A/B against the source from anywhere — not just the Equalizer. Under the hood, the audio engine now shrugs off the transient device hiccups that could leave it silent after a wake or a route change.

Added

  • New app icon. A dimensional gold magnifying glass over a frequency spectrum — sharper at every size from the Dock down to the menu bar.
  • Reference Mode in the title bar. The Bypass toggle moved out of the Equalizer and into the window toolbar, so you can drop to the unprocessed source from any screen. It's renamed Reference Mode to match the popover and ⌘B — one control, three places, same wording. Goes red when active so you always know you're hearing raw audio.

Changed

  • Liquid Glass chrome (macOS Tahoe). On macOS 26 the toolbar controls now render as separate Liquid Glass clusters, the notice banner and layer chips pick up the glass material, and detail content softly fades as it scrolls under the toolbar. Sonoma and Sequoia keep their existing look.
  • Steadier sidebars. Both the navigation sidebar and the monitor gutter are now pinned to a fixed 240 pt and stay put — no width drift between launches, and the primary navigation no longer collapses out from under you.

Fixed

  • Silent engine after sleep or a route change. When the audio device reports a transient "try again" error — common while a sample-rate or output-route change is still settling, or right after waking from sleep — SherlockEQ now retries the engine start automatically instead of surfacing an error and going quiet.

Not a medical device

SherlockEQ is not a healthcare or medical application. It does not diagnose, treat, measure, or monitor any hearing condition, tinnitus, or disability. For concerns about your hearing, consult a doctor, audiologist, or licensed healthcare professional.

item.title: SherlockEQ 0.1.3
item.description:
SherlockEQ 0.1.3

A pass over every Equalizer tab — the input (pre-EQ) and post-EQ spectra now ride together behind the curve so you can see what your correction is actually doing to your music in real time. Advanced gets the layer chip strip and tap-to-type gain chips that used to be Expert-only, and a dedicated Bypass button finally lives on the Equalizer surface itself.

Added

  • Live input + post-EQ spectrum overlay. The dry input and the post-EQ output spectra are now both rendered behind the EQ curve on every Equalizer tab — Simple, Speech, Advanced, and Expert. The input layer used to be Expert-only (and off by default); it's now on by default everywhere. The overlay also takes up more of the canvas (50 % → 70 % vertical) so it reads as a real background fill rather than a thin ribbon at the bottom.
  • Bypass button on the Equalizer. A pill toggle now sits at the top of every Equalizer tab — flip it to A/B between your tuning and the raw source without leaving the screen. Goes red + "Bypassed" when active so you can't lose track of which state you're in. Drives the same Reference Mode that ⌘B and the popover already used; nothing new to learn.
  • Layer chip strip on Advanced. Advanced now exposes the same Input / Output / EQ curve / Audiogram target / Safety overlay / Peak callouts chips that Expert has had. Your chip preferences are shared across the two modes — what you toggle in one shows up the same way in the other.
  • Tap-to-type gain chips on Advanced. Each of Advanced's ten octave bands now shows its current gain in a small editable chip above the slider. Tap it, type a value ("+2.5", "−3", "0", a trailing "dB" is fine), press Return — or just click anywhere outside the chip and it commits. Esc cancels. Keyboard nudges (±0.5 dB) work for VoiceOver users too.

Not a medical device

SherlockEQ is not a healthcare or medical application. It does not diagnose, treat, measure, or monitor any hearing condition, tinnitus, or disability. For concerns about your hearing, consult a doctor, audiologist, or licensed healthcare professional.

item.title: SherlockEQ 0.1.2
item.description:
SherlockEQ 0.1.2

Moves the system-audio permission into Apple's narrower "System Audio Recording" bucket on macOS 15+, makes audio-engine failures actually tell you what went wrong, and bumps the minimum window size so the Equalizer and Tinnitus Notch screens fit without scrolling.

Changed

  • Permission moved to "System Audio Recording". Previously SherlockEQ asked for "Screen & System Audio Recording" — the same broad permission used by screen-recording apps like Loom and Microsoft Teams. macOS 15 Sequoia introduced a narrower, audio-only TCC bucket called "System Audio Recording" — where Audio Hijack and Audio Routing Kit live — and SherlockEQ now uses that instead. On macOS 14, it appears under Screen Recording in Settings (Apple hadn't split the UI yet); on macOS 15+, it has its own row.
  • Minimum window size bumped (1400×740 → 1400×860). The Equalizer and Tinnitus Notch screens now fit without scrolling at the smallest allowed size.

Fixed

  • "Graph not attached" replaced with the real reason. When the audio engine failed to start, the banner used to say "Audio engine: Graph not attached" — a generic message that masked the actual problem (a format build failure, an unexpected sample-rate mismatch). The engine now surfaces the specific cause so the notice is actionable.

If you installed 0.1.0 or 0.1.1

On first launch after upgrading, macOS will prompt for the new "System Audio Recording" permission. Grant it, then quit and relaunch SherlockEQ — TCC permissions don't take effect for a running process until the next launch.

Your previous grant under "Screen & System Audio Recording" is orphaned but harmless. If you want to clean it up: System Settings → Privacy & Security → Screen & System Audio Recording → select SherlockEQ → click the minus button. Optional.

Not a medical device

SherlockEQ is not a healthcare or medical application. It does not diagnose, treat, measure, or monitor any hearing condition, tinnitus, or disability. For concerns about your hearing, consult a doctor, audiologist, or licensed healthcare professional.

Previous release

See the 0.1.1 release notes for what shipped in the prior version.

item.title: SherlockEQ 0.1.1
item.description:
SherlockEQ 0.1.1

Bug-fix release. Two surfaces in 0.1.0 shipped without Info.plist keys they needed; both are fixed here. No feature changes.

Fixed

  • Check for Updates now works. The 0.1.0 bundle was missing SUFeedURL and SUPublicEDKey, so Sparkle surfaced an "Update Error" dialog and refused to check. Both keys are present in 0.1.1; signature verification is wired against this app's EdDSA public key.
  • Screen Recording permission prompt is now properly explained. macOS requires a usage description (NSScreenCaptureUsageDescription) for any app that captures system audio through Core Audio Taps. 0.1.0 was missing it, which made the prompt either silent or empty depending on macOS version, and the app could not get past the gate even after enabling the permission in System Settings. The usage description is present in 0.1.1 and macOS now prompts with a clear explanation.

Changed

  • The build number (CFBundleVersion) is now derived from the marketing version by the release pipeline, so the bundle and the Sparkle appcast stay in sync across future bumps without manual intervention.

If you installed 0.1.0

After upgrading, clear the stale TCC entries so macOS re-prompts with the new usage descriptions: 

tccutil reset ScreenCapture com.shawnbrown.SherlockEQ
tccutil reset Microphone    com.shawnbrown.SherlockEQ

Then quit SherlockEQ from the menu bar and relaunch. macOS shows the Screen Recording prompt with the usage string. Approve it, then quit and relaunch one more time — Screen Recording does not take effect for a running process until the next launch.

Not a medical device

SherlockEQ is not a healthcare or medical application. It does not diagnose, treat, measure, or monitor any hearing condition, tinnitus, or disability. For concerns about your hearing, consult a doctor, audiologist, or licensed healthcare professional.

0.1.0 changelog

For the full feature list shipped at 0.1.0, see the 0.1.0 release notes.

item.title: SherlockEQ 0.1.0
item.description:
SherlockEQ 0.1.0

First public release. SherlockEQ is a per-ear audio equalizer for macOS, useful for anyone who wants better control over how their Mac sounds — not only listeners with hearing differences or tinnitus. It taps system audio through Apple's native Core Audio Tap API. No virtual driver, no kernel extension, no audio-routing setup. Use the master gain by itself, or layer in audiogram-shaped curves, tinnitus notch filtering, AutoEQ headphone correction, and dose tracking — as few or as many features as you want.

What's in 0.1

Equalization

  • Independent left and right EQ chains, implemented as Direct Form II Transposed biquad cascades. No AVAudioUnitEQ on the user-signal path — real per-channel separation, not coupled stereo processing.
  • Four EQ modes per profile: Simple (bass / mid / treble shelves), Speech (six speech-frequency bands with presets), Advanced (ten octave-spaced parametric bands), and Expert (any band, any frequency, any filter type — keyboard-driven).
  • AutoEQ headphone correction upstream of the profile EQ. Imports the standard ParametricEQ.txt format.
  • Master output gain with a dedicated post-limiter stage (-60 dB to +24 dB) and per-profile stereo balance.

Tinnitus

  • Continuous-phase sine sweep across 20 Hz to 20 kHz, fine-tunable to one hertz.
  • Per-ear notch filtering. Set the tone for the left ear, the right ear, or both.

Audiogram

  • Per-ear threshold entry on a log-frequency chart.
  • Translated into an EQ curve in real time with severity bars and a live preview.

Safety

  • NIOSH dose tracking with a remaining-time readout smoothed over short transients (60-second EMA in the power domain).
  • Per-frequency safety overlay on the spectrum, calibration-aware.
  • Menu-bar dose tint and notifications at warning and danger thresholds.
  • Apple AUPeakLimiter on the output bus.

Workflow

  • Menu-bar popover with master gain, balance, profile picker, level meters, and a reference-mode bypass.
  • Main window with profile management, audiogram entry, four EQ surfaces, tinnitus tone finder, safe listening dashboard, and a persistent right-side monitor sidebar.
  • Profile import and export. Undo and redo with per-band coalescing.
  • Built-in profiles cannot be edited; duplicate to customize.
  • Device auto-switch when a profile is linked to an output.

Accessibility

  • VoiceOver and keyboard control across every custom canvas and drag surface, including audiogram entry, EQ band sliders, and the tinnitus sweep.
  • Color-blind redundant encoding on safety zones (icon plus position, not just color).
  • Reduced-motion guards on transitions. Dynamic Type respected on labels.

What's not in 0.1

  • Onboarding wizard. First launch goes straight to the main UI; you will be prompted for Microphone and Screen & System Audio Recording permissions cold. The second prompt is non-obvious — macOS requires it for any system-audio capture. SherlockEQ does not record video or screen contents.
  • Localization beyond English. The String Catalog infrastructure is in place; translations are not yet wired.
  • Spectrogram visualization. Code is present but disabled pending a performance and UX revision.

Requirements

  • macOS 14.6 or later
  • Apple Silicon or Intel (universal binary)
  • Microphone permission and Screen & System Audio Recording permission

Not a medical device

SherlockEQ is not a healthcare or medical application. It does not diagnose, treat, measure, or monitor any hearing condition, tinnitus, or disability. For concerns about your hearing, consult a doctor, audiologist, or licensed healthcare professional.

Acknowledgments

NIOSH dose math. Audio EQ Cookbook (Robert Bristow-Johnson) for biquad coefficients. AutoEQ project, oratory1990, and Crinacle for headphone correction profiles.
